assessment.nobel_worthiness: Methods for estimating demand with differentiated products, market power and dynamic industry equilibrium now underpin merger review, antitrust, trade, health and environmental analysis. Their reach well beyond IO is the main basis for this ranking, and I judge it a very strong case.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes built the random-coefficients demand framework. Pakes also led dynamic oligopoly estimation, including Ericson-Pakes and the work with Benkard. Bresnahan led the New Empirical IO tradition of inferring market power from data. Reiss, Levin, Benkard and Levinsohn are also credited, so the three-name limit forces a hard choice and risks leaving out Levinsohn.
assessment.maturity: The core contributions date from the 1980s to the 2000s. They have been used heavily for decades and have had a documented effect on policy practice. There is no timing concern.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to credit Levinsohn over Bresnahan, or to treat the demand-estimation and dynamic-games strands as one contribution.
Whether a prize for IO methods is seen as too narrow given past recognition of related work, and how recent recognition of adjacent fields affects the choice.
My own IO background could make me overrate this field, so I rely on the breadth of its use as the common criterion.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting changed how trade economists think about gains from trade, the margins of adjustment and productivity reallocation. It has been very influential in theory and in empirical work on firm-level data.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central, widely cited model. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple extended it to exports versus FDI. Helpman also has a long record in new trade theory and in political economy. Redding is credited for quantitative spatial and trade work. A Melitz-Helpman pair is natural, but the credit relative to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on this ballot, is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: The work is more than twenty years old, with a large empirical literature validating the main predictions. Krugman's 2008 prize covers earlier trade theory, so this is a separate contribution.
uncertainties: Credit relative to Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum, who are not credited here, and to Eaton-Kortum.
Whether Helpman's body of work or only the firm-heterogeneity strand is being rewarded.
Overlap with other trade candidates on the list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with nominal rigidities, microfounded Phillips curves and the Taylor rule, is the standard analytical basis for modern monetary policy and central-bank practice. Its policy influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: This is highly diffuse. Calvo, Taylor, Rotemberg, Woodford, Gali, Gertler, Clarida and Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans each contributed distinct pieces. Woodford synthesised the framework, Gali developed its empirical and theoretical applications, and Taylor supplied the rule. Any three-name selection will omit key contributors, and that difficulty weakens the case.
assessment.maturity: The work is fully mature, with decades of use in central banks. The 2025 and earlier prizes did not cover it directly.
uncertainties: Attribution is the main obstacle, and the proposed trio is contestable.
Some committees would prefer a narrower theme, such as pricing frictions, to this broad framework.
Post-2021 inflation experience could sharpen or complicate the assessment of the framework.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The empirical sufficient-statistics approach to taxation, built on elasticities of taxable income, bunching and behavioural responses, links theory to evidence and has changed policy discussion on top rates and tax design.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod and Feldstein (not credited) were early on taxable-income responses. Saez developed the optimal-tax and top-income applications and Chetty the sufficient-statistics framework. Stantcheva's work is more recent. Saez and Chetty also appear in other candidates, which makes credit overlapping and harder to separate.
assessment.maturity: The core work spans about 1990 to 2015 and is well replicated. The policy impact is documented, although the research programme is still developing.
uncertainties: Feldstein's role as originator is not represented in the credited names.
Overlap of credited individuals with the inequality and mobility candidates.
Replication and external validity of elasticity estimates across contexts.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China shock evidence reshaped understanding of labour-market polarisation, trade adjustment and regional effects. The work has had major policy and public influence.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure across both the task framework (with Levy and Murnane, and with Acemoglu) and the China shock work (with Dorn and Hanson). Acemoglu is not credited here and has already received a prize. Katz is credited for earlier skill-biased change research.
assessment.maturity: The China shock papers date from 2013 to 2016 and have generated a large literature, with some continuing debate about magnitude. The measurement of long-run effects is still developing.
uncertainties: Persistent debate about the size and persistence of the China shock effects.
Acemoglu's overlap, and whether the committee would split the task and trade strands.
Lower theoretical novelty than some other candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Diffusion-index and dynamic factor forecasting, together with work on identification in macroeconometrics, supplied core tools used by central banks and macro forecasters. The contribution is methodological but widely used.
assessment.attribution: Stock and Watson's diffusion-index forecasting and their related work are the clearest credit. Reichlin and co-authors (Forni, Hallin, Lippi) developed the generalised dynamic factor approach in parallel. Diebold, Mariano and West are linked to forecast evaluation, which is a separate strand.
assessment.maturity: The work is about twenty-five years old and in routine use. The timing is fine.
uncertainties: Parallel invention by Reichlin and co-authors complicates priority.
The bundle mixes factor models with forecast evaluation, which are distinct contributions.
Econometrics prizes are rare and the committee may have a high bar for methods.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The intertemporal approach to the current account, the Redux model of open-economy macroeconomics with nominal rigidities, and the exchange-rate disconnect puzzle laid the foundations for modern international macro. My own work on pass-through and invoicing makes me aware of how central these frameworks are to the field, and also of how many questions remain open.
assessment.attribution: Obstfeld and Rogoff's 1995 Redux paper and their textbook are central. Others, such as Lane, Devereux, Engel and Gopinath, extended the framework and are not credited. Rogoff also appears in the financial-crisis history candidate, so his credit is spread across several strands.
assessment.maturity: The work is mature and has become standard in graduate teaching. The disconnect puzzles remain partly unresolved, which limits how definitive the contribution is.
uncertainties: Open puzzles such as exchange-rate disconnect may make the contribution look incomplete.
Influence on policy practice is less direct than for monetary or tax work.
Credit overlap with Rogoff's other candidate and with later contributors such as Gopinath.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The microfoundations of agglomeration, with sharing, matching and learning, plus evidence on city growth and housing supply, is a substantial body of work on a core question of economic geography, complementing Krugman's earlier prize.
assessment.attribution: Duranton and Puga formalised the microfoundations of urban agglomeration and Glaeser contributed influential empirical and conceptual work on cities and human capital. Moretti and Gyourko cover local labour-market effects and housing. Fujita, Henderson and others made foundational contributions and are not credited.
assessment.maturity: The work is mature and has had clear policy influence on housing and zoning debates. Recent empirical work is still growing.
uncertainties: Foundational credit to Fujita, Henderson and others outside the credited names.
Heterogeneity of the field makes it hard to isolate a single discovery.
Mixed theory and empirical credit across the five credited names.
